title: How Toppers Score GPA 4.0 in SEE: A 90-Day Blueprint
excerpt: The exact study routine, resource plan and revision strategy followed by national toppers — from mock test frequency to sleep schedules.
author: Bhawana Ghimire
body: Scoring a perfect 4.0 in SEE is not about being gifted — it is about a deliberate system. After interviewing thirty national toppers over five years, the pattern is unmistakable.

Phase one is syllabus mapping. Download the official CDC grid and assign weightage to each unit based on past papers. Algebra and Geometry in maths, and Electricity and Chemistry in science deserve the most hours because they carry the largest marks.

Phase two is the 50/30/20 rule. Spend 50% of your study time actively solving questions, 30% revising formulas and concepts, and only 20% reading new material. Active retrieval is the single biggest predictor of board performance.

Mock tests change everything. Toppers attempt at least one full-length timed mock per week from Baishakh onwards, then spend the following day analyzing every error. A missed mark is a gift — it reveals exactly what to revise.

Finally, protect your body. 7 hours of sleep, 30 minutes of exercise and scheduled breaks outperform any late-night cramming. Your brain consolidates learning while you sleep, so a rested mind is your real secret weapon.

title: The Ultimate Grade 12 Science Study Plan for NEB 2083
excerpt: A week-by-week plan balancing Physics, Chemistry, Biology and Maths so you enter the NEB hall confident.
author: Rohit K.C.
body: Grade 12 is the most consequential year of the +2 track — your NEB score shapes engineering, medical and CSIT entrance prospects. The winning plan balances theory depth with numerical fluency.

Week 1-6 focus on derivations. Physics and Chemistry toppers write every derivation from memory three times before touching numericals. Biology demands diagram-perfect answers; practice each labelled diagram until it takes under five minutes.

Week 7-14 switch to mixed practice. Solve NEB-pattern numericals daily — at least five from Physics and three from Chemistry. Use unit-wise question banks and mark your error rate per unit to identify weak zones early.
Week 15-20 are full mocks. Attempt complete papers under real timing each Saturday, then revise the Sunday error log. This is when your grade is truly decided.
Beyond academics, register your entrance exams early, keep transcripts ready, and use Sandarbh's mock tests that mirror the exact NEB paper structure.

title: BSc CSIT Semester Survival Guide: Notes, Papers & Projects
excerpt: How TU CSIT students navigate eight semesters of programming, theory and endless deadlines without burning out.
author: Aashish Shrestha
body: CSIT at TU is equal parts thrilling and relentless. Eight semesters, dozens of theory papers and a constant demand for projects — the students who thrive are the ones with systems.

Semester 1-2 are make-or-break. C Programming and Digital Logic feel alien at first, but they build the mental model for everything after. Code daily, even 30 minutes, and never let a lab assignment pile up.

From semester 3, the classic 'old-is-gold' strategy wins: previous-year question papers are your syllabus. The exam pattern barely changes, so practice with past papers and identify the recurring topics.
Projects earn you more than grades. A solid web or mobile project in semesters 6-7 becomes your interview portfolio. Collaborate, use version control, and document everything.

title: Every Scholarship in Nepal You Should Apply For (2026)
excerpt: A curated roundup of government, private and international scholarships with deadlines, amounts and eligibility.
author: Sujata Rijal
body: Nepali students leave lakhs of rupees on the table every year simply because they don't know what's available. This guide maps the landscape.

Government quotas are the most underused. CTEVT, NEB and university constituent colleges reserve 20-30% of seats for marginalized groups, girls and economically disadvantaged students — but applications are sparse.

Private foundations reward merit and need together. Organizations like the Sushil Koirala Memorial Foundation, Rotary Clubs and university alumni funds publish detailed criteria every Shrawan and Bhadra.
The golden rule: start three months before the deadline. Transcripts, recommendations and essays all take time, and late applications are rejected outright.
Set a reminder for every deadline in Sandarbh's Scholarship section, and don't apply for just one — apply for five.

title: Why the Pomodoro Technique Works for Board Exams
excerpt: The neuroscience behind 25-minute focus sprints and how to use them for SEE, NEB and entrance preparation.
author: Kiran Dulal
body: Your attention span works in waves, not endless streams. The Pomodoro technique — 25 minutes of deep focus followed by a 5-minute break — aligns your study rhythm with how your brain actually functions.
The 25-minute window is long enough to enter a focused state but short enough that procrastination feels surmountable. Starting a session is the hardest part, and a short timer makes starting easy.
During breaks, don't reach for your phone. Walk, stretch or hydrate. Dopamine-triggering screens interrupt the consolidation your brain does between sessions.
Use the technique for active recall: one pomodoro to attempt 10 questions, one to check answers and log errors, one to revise the formula sheet. Three sprints beat three hours of passive rereading.

title: Science, Management, Humanities or CTEVT? Choosing the Right Faculty
excerpt: A framework to choose your +2 and bachelor's path based on interests, aptitude, family and career outcomes.
author: Dr. Meena Shrestha
body: Choosing a faculty is the first big life decision for most Nepali students, and too many make it on hearsay. Here is a framework that actually works.

Start with aptitude, not prestige. Love building and solving puzzles? Science and engineering suit you. Drawn to people, markets and numbers? Management and BBA. Hands-on and practical? CTEVT diplomas lead to careers in as little as three years.

Second, map the outcomes honestly. Engineering and health open specific professional tracks with entrance exams and licensing. Management is broader and pairs well with entrepreneurship. Humanities feed education, law, journalism and civil service.
Third, talk to people who live those lives. One conversation with a nurse, engineer or accountant teaches you more than a hundred brochures.
Finally, remember this is reversible. Transfer routes, entrance exams and post-graduate paths let you course-correct. Choose with information, not pressure.
